::: {#rem-collision-entropy}
#### The expected probability is the collision probability

Entropy averages the [surprisal](#def-surprisal) $-\log \P(X)$ over the outcomes of $X$.
Averaging the probability $\P(X)$ itself gives a different summary of the same distribution.
For a discrete random variable $X$, let $X'$ be an independent copy of $X$.
Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{\P(X)}
&= \sum_x \P(X=x)^2 \\
&= \P(X = X').
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the **collision probability**, the chance that two independent draws are equal.
For a continuous random variable with density $\p$, the analogue is $\E{\p(X)} = \int \p(x)^2\,dx$,
which the [expected-density exercise](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#exr-expected-density) computes
for the uniform and normal distributions.

The **Rényi entropy of order 2**, also called the **collision entropy**, is the negative logarithm of this quantity
[@wikipedia_renyi_entropy]:

$$H_2(X) = -\log \E{\P(X)}.$$

It is smaller than or equal to the Shannon entropy $\entropyf{X} = \E{-\log \P(X)}$,
because $-\log$ is a convex function and Jensen's inequality gives $\E{-\log \P(X)} \ge -\log \E{\P(X)}$.
The two are equal when $X$ is uniform on a finite set,
since then $\P(X)$ takes the same value for every outcome.

:::
